blocks.text: Largely unseen, Sanlé Sory ’s colour photography is on show for the first time in the UK at The Photographers’ Gallery this autumn in Sanlé Sory: Colour Years .

One of West Africa’s most prolific photographers, Sanlé Sory (b. 1943, Burkina Faso) took an estimated million photographs over six decades, showing the profound social and political changes in Burkina Faso. Colour Years captures a lesser-known chapter of his career. His colour prints, meticulously restored from the negatives in his archive, will be on show, alongside Volta Jazz album covers featuring his portraits of the influential bands that flourished after Burkina Faso’s independence.

Better known for his black-and-white studio photography of the 1960s and 70s, Sanlé Sory started producing colour portraits in his Volta Photo studio in the mid-1980s. Colour Years reveals a dynamic portrait of a rapidly changing community and society in Burkina Faso across decades of political shifts, global exchange and self-expression through fashion, music and attitude.

When asked why he moved over to colour, Sory said, “When you are in a place where everybody dances, you have to try to dance like everyone else!” His clients wanted a new way to see and show themselves, and he gave it to them.

Sanlé Sory first came to photography when he needed an identity photograph. After several years learning his trade as an apprentice, he set up his own studio in 1960 when he was 17. He kitted his studio out with props and hand-painted backdrops to attract clients in his hometown of Bobo-Dioulasso. His clients chose their clothes, hairstyles, props and poses with great care. However, his portraits are about more than fashion and style. They tell a story of everyday life after the huge changes brought by the country’s independence from France.

From studio portraits of families, couples and friends, to identity photographs and portraits of traders and shopkeepers in the local market, Sory’s photographs are a vivid portrait of a country in transition and a community ready to embrace change.

Sanlé Sory (b. 1943, Burkina Faso) is best known for the black and white studio and nightlife photographs he made in Bobo-Dioulasso, Burkina Faso, from the 1960s. He opened the Volta Photo studio in 1960 – the same year Upper Volta (now Burkina Faso) was navigating independence. His photography mixed formal studio portraiture with on-the-street reportage of the city’s music, dance halls and youth culture. In response to his clients, he moved over to colour photography in the mid-1980s.

Though his work was little known internationally for decades, Sory’s photographs have been the subject of major exhibitions including Volta Photo: Starring Sanlé Sory and the People of Bobo-Dioulasso at the Art Institute of Chicago in 2018 and are now included in museum collections and galleries worldwide.
Sanlé Sory: Colour Years is curated by Taous Dahmani, Curator at The Photographers’ Gallery, and produced by The Photographers’ Gallery.
With thanks to Florent Mazzoleni and the Sanlé Sory Archive for the generous loan of the works and to Sanlé Sory for his collaboration.
Sanlé Sory: Colour Years Until February 21, 2027 The Photographers’ Gallery 16–18 Ramillies Street London W1F 7LW www.tpg.org.uk
